where: exam traps, trap 3 (also relates to section 2, turbulent flat-plate correlation)
problem: The trap claims Sh = 0.037 Re^0.8 Sc^(1/3) 'already averages a plate that starts laminar at the leading edge'. Standard texts treat this fit as turbulent flow from the leading edge; the mixed laminar-then-turbulent plate is described by Sh = (0.037 Re^0.8 − 871) Sc^(1/3). At the lower end of the stated range (Re = 5×10⁵) the two differ by about a factor of three, so a student who follows the trap will report a badly wrong Sh and k_c.
fix: Say: Sh = 0.037 Re^0.8 Sc^(1/3) assumes the boundary layer is turbulent from the leading edge; for a plate that is laminar near the nose and turbulent further on, use Sh = (0.037 Re^0.8 − 871) Sc^(1/3). Keep the warning 'do not add a laminar term' but note the correction is a subtraction, not an addition.

problem: The laminar curve is drawn to Re = 10⁶ although the text says it holds below about 5×10⁵, and the turbulent curve is drawn from Re = 10⁴ although the text says it holds from about 5×10⁵ to 10⁷. The plot therefore shows exactly the extrapolation the section warns against, and a student may read off values outside the fitted bands.
fix: Plot the laminar line only up to Re ≈ 5×10⁵ and start the turbulent line at Re ≈ 5×10⁵, or extend both but add to the caption that the lines are drawn past their validity bands only for visual comparison.

problem: 'Gas diffusivities give Sc near 0.6 to 1' is too narrow. Gases span roughly 0.2 (hydrogen or helium in air) to about 3; 0.6 to 1 covers only common pairs such as water vapour in air.
fix: 'For gases Sc usually lies between about 0.2 and 3, near 0.6 for water vapour in air; in liquids Sc reaches hundreds or thousands.'

where: section 2, sentence after the sphere formula
problem: 'All three are empirical fits to the same boundary-layer problem' is not accurate. The two flat-plate fits come from boundary-layer theory on a plate; the sphere fit (Ranz–Marshall type) is an empirical correlation for a completely different geometry, which is why it has the additive term 2.
fix: 'The first two are boundary-layer fits for a flat plate; the sphere fit is an empirical correlation for a different geometry. Sc^(1/3) appears in all three because the laminar sublayer near the surface controls the mass transfer resistance in each case.'

problem: 'Convection adds to diffusion, so the flux is written N_A = k_c Δc' suggests the flux is a sum of two separate contributions. N_A = k_c Δc is a definition of the coefficient, and mixing raises k_c by steepening the near-wall concentration gradient; the 'so' will confuse a reader meeting this for the first time.
fix: 'The flux at the surface is still diffusive, N_A = k_c Δc, but stirring steepens the concentration gradient near the wall and so raises k_c. Compare this with the purely diffusive flux D_AB Δc/L over the same length; the ratio is the Sherwood number.'
